title: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) maternal vaccination coverage in England: May 2026 report - GOV.UK

analysis.time: The report was published on 1 October 2026. The data refers to the period up to May 2026, with the vaccine uptake measured for women who delivered in May 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The report focuses on England, specifically on NHS commissioning regions and integrated care boards (ICBs) within the country. It includes data on pregnant women across different ethnic groups.
analysis.event: The report details the maternal RSV vaccination coverage in England as of May 2026, including uptake rates by NHS commissioning region, ICB, and ethnic group. It is an official statistics release by the UK Health Security Agency.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The RSV vaccine uptake in May 2026 was 62.2% among women who delivered during that month. Uptake varied significantly by region, with the highest at 72.3% in the South West and lowest at 54.8% in London. It also varied by ICB, with the highest at 76.3% in Norfolk and Waveney and lowest at 41.1% in Birmingham and Solihull. Ethnic group differences were also noted, with the highest uptake among the Asian or Asian British - Chinese group (78.5%) and lowest among the Black - Caribbean group (39.2%).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report is an official statistics release and includes data from both major GP IT suppliers, covering 98.7% of GPs in England. It notes improvements in data quality and a more representative analysis of uptake since January 2025. The data is based on a three-month reporting lag to ensure completeness and accuracy.

analysis.brief_en: The UK Health Security Agency released an official statistics report on 1 October 2026 detailing the maternal RSV vaccination coverage in England as of May 2026. The report highlights that 62.2% of pregnant women who delivered in May 2026 received the RSV vaccine, with regional variations observed. The highest uptake was recorded in the South West region at 72.3%, while London had the lowest at 54.8%. Integrated care boards (ICBs) also showed significant differences, with Norfolk and Waveney reporting 76.3% uptake and Birmingham and Solihull at 41.1%. Ethnic group disparities were noted, with the Asian or Asian British - Chinese group having the highest uptake at 78.5% and the Black - Caribbean group the lowest at 39.2%. The data, collected from 98.7% of GPs in England, reflects improvements in data quality since January 2025, allowing for a more representative analysis of vaccine coverage. The report serves as a monitoring tool for the national immunisation programme targeting RSV-related illnesses in infants and older adults.

analysis.time: The study was conducted from September 2023 to June 2025, with follow-up assessments occurring in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study took place in Madrid, Spain, involving 185 children and adolescents aged 5-18 years who had been hospitalized for severe bronchiolitis caused by RSV subgroup A or B during their first 2 years of life.
analysis.event: A study found that children hospitalized for bronchiolitis caused by RSV-B were more likely to report severe wheezing that restricted speech and nighttime dry cough at school age compared to those with RSV-A, based on a Spanish-validated asthma symptom questionnaire.

The research, conducted in Madrid, Spain, from September 2023 to June 2025, included 185 children aged 5-18 years who had been hospitalized for bronchiolitis due to a single RSV infection during their first two years of life. The study used a Spanish-validated asthma symptom questionnaire to assess respiratory outcomes. While severe wheezing and nighttime dry cough were more common in the RSV-B group, current asthma prevalence, lung function, exhaled nitric oxide levels, and allergic sensitization were not significantly different between the two groups. The study had limitations, including a smaller RSV-B sample size and reliance on recall-based symptom reporting, which may have introduced bias. The authors suggest that closer monitoring of children with a history of RSV-B bronchiolitis could lead to better management of respiratory symptoms and reduced medium-term morbidity.
